title: Smart Irrigation
metaTitle: Smart Irrigation: Soil Monitoring & Remote Control | Hitelecom
description: Connect soil moisture, pressure, flow and weather with Hitelecom IoT controllers. Operate compatible irrigation valves and pumps, then verify water delivery.

hero.heading: Smart irrigation.
hero.intro: Know when a block needs water, operate compatible valves or pump controls through Hitelecom IoT controllers, and check the result with position, flow, pressure and root-zone feedback.
hero.alt: Open agricultural fields with crop rows and irrigation management zones

problem.heading:
The schedule ran.
Did the field receive the water?
problem.intro: Match three pieces of evidence: what the soil needed, what the system delivered and how the root zone responded.

cards.title: Demand varies across the field
cards.body: Soil texture, crop stage and root depth change watering needs. One timer or one probe cannot represent every management block.

cards.title: A command is not delivered water
cards.body: An open command cannot confirm valve position, pump operation or flow. Feedback distinguishes a missed action from poor distribution.

cards.title: Supply and weather can change
cards.body: A low tank, new rainfall or a pressure loss can make the planned cycle unsuitable. Check those conditions before the next operation.

problem.takeaway: Which block needs water, which needs a delivery inspection, and what evidence supports that choice?

focus.heading:
From a dry root zone
to a verified watering cycle.
focus.intro: Link the zone measurement, the authorised command and the physical result. Keep each irrigation block identifiable throughout.

stages.title: Measure the need
stages.body: Read representative root-zone moisture, rainfall and available water. Use crop-specific references to decide whether to irrigate.

stages.title: Operate the selected zone
stages.body: Use a commissioned Hitelecom IoT controller to command compatible valve actuators or pump control circuits, remotely or through configured rules.

stages.title: Verify delivery
stages.body: Check valve position or pump run feedback, then flow, pressure and the root-zone response. Investigate any mismatch.

focus.note: Controller output, valve position and water flow are different signals. A command acknowledgement alone does not prove that irrigation occurred.
focus.detailTitle: What makes a remote irrigation loop dependable?
focus.detail: Specify the valve or pump interface, output electrical limits, position or run feedback and the meter data route. Agree any schedule or condition-based logic, maximum run time, manual override, dry-run protection and loss-of-network or power behaviour. Keep necessary local interlocks with the host equipment. Test start, stop, failed feedback and restoration on a representative zone before enabling unattended operation.

applications.heading:

applications.intro: Use the same measurement logic with a different point layout for each crop and irrigation system.

deployment.heading:
Make the first irrigation cycle

steps.title: Map demand & delivery
steps.body: Share crop blocks, water source, valve and pump electrical interfaces, existing meters and required remote operating tasks.

steps.title: Install & align the records
steps.body: Map soil, pressure, flow and level to each zone. Configure controller I/O, permitted commands and feedback; retain required local safeguards.

steps.body: Test start and stop, position or run confirmation, water delivery and soil response. Demonstrate manual override and agreed failure behaviour.

acceptance: Soil points, sensing depths and delivery points match the same zone plan.
Soil and pressure reference checks are recorded; weather exposure is appropriate.
Start / stop, physical feedback, maximum run time and agreed failure-response tests are documented.
The operator verifies delivery and soil response during a real cycle; control permissions and local protection are handed over.

faq.q: What does Smart Irrigation include beyond a soil-moisture sensor?
faq.a: The solution can combine representative soil points, pressure, a compatible flow meter, rainfall and tank level with a Hitelecom IoT controller. The operator can command a compatible zone and verify valve or pump feedback, actual delivery and soil response. Select the measurements around the irrigation layout; every point does not need every sensor.

faq.q: Can one moisture threshold work across the whole farm?
faq.a: Usually not. Soil, root depth, crop stage and delivery capacity change how a reading should be interpreted. Set review levels with the grower or agronomist using site references. Keep separate management blocks where conditions differ, and review the levels as the crop develops.

faq.q: How can the team distinguish poor delivery from a dry soil trend?
faq.a: Compare the soil response with pressure, any available flow record and the irrigation event for that block. A mismatch identifies where to investigate; it does not identify the fault by itself. Check emitters, valves, probe contact and local soil conditions before changing the schedule.

faq.q: Can Hitelecom remotely switch irrigation valves and pumps?
faq.a: Yes, through a suitable Hitelecom IoT controller and compatible equipment interface. The HD20-4000 reference configuration includes digital outputs for command circuits, digital inputs for position or run/fault feedback, and analogue inputs. It is not a universal direct power supply for valves or motors. Match the electrical interface, actuator power, control permissions and local interlocks to the installed equipment.

faq.q: Can watering use a schedule or soil-moisture rule?
faq.a: Scheduled or condition-based operation can be configured within the supplied control scope. Define the crop reference, data freshness, maximum run time, available water, manual override and independent local pump protection. Verify loss-of-network and loss-of-power behaviour with the actual controller and host equipment; the presence of an IoT controller alone does not confirm an autonomous offline irrigation programme.

faq.q: What confirms that a remote command worked?
faq.a: Use a valve end-position or pump run input where available, then compare flow and pressure with the expected cycle. These confirm different parts of the process. A command acknowledgement shows communications or command handling; it does not establish physical valve movement or delivered volume. The later soil response adds evidence at the monitored root zone.

faq.q: Can EC, pH or nutrient measurements determine fertiliser dosing?
faq.a: These channels can support a soil investigation when their configuration, range and reference method suit the site. They do not replace an agronomic testing programme. Fertiliser or fertigation decisions need the crop plan, appropriate soil or solution tests and the responsible agronomist’s interpretation.

faq.q: How does this differ from Smart Greenhouses?
faq.a: Smart Irrigation centres on field blocks, water delivery and root-zone response. Smart Greenhouses also examines the enclosed growing climate: canopy temperature, humidity, selected CO₂, outside weather and climate-system context. Substrate-based growing needs its own probe suitability and reference checks.
